```{r, include = FALSE}
options(width = 100)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
library(AgriDesign)
```

Before the trial: how many replicates, which design, and where each treatment
goes in the field.

## How many replicates?

The number of replicates depends on the coefficient of variation expected (take
it from earlier trials of the same crop and site) and on the smallest
difference worth detecting. `power_design()` uses the noncentral t
distribution with the error degrees of freedom of the design:

```{r}
pw <- power_design(cv = 12, diff = 15, t = 6, design = "rcbd")
pw
plot(pw)
```

Halving the coefficient of variation is worth as much as quadrupling the
replicates: uniform land, plots of the right size, border rows and blocks laid
across the gradient are usually cheaper than more plots.

## Randomising the layout

`make_design()` randomises sixteen designs. The randomisation is reproducible
with `seed` and does not change the random state of the session.

```{r}
lay <- make_design("rcbd", trt = c("N0", "N60", "N120", "N180", "N240"), r = 4, seed = 2026)
lay
plot(lay)
```

Split-plots keep the main plots together and randomise inside them:

```{r}
sp <- make_design("split_rcbd", A = c("Drip", "Furrow"), B = paste0("V", 1:4), r = 3,
                  seed = 2026, arrangement = "side", blocks_per_row = 3)
plot(sp)
```

## Incomplete blocks

With many entries, complete blocks become large and heterogeneous. Alpha
designs split each replicate into small blocks; `make_design()` searches the
alpha array with the highest efficiency factor, which `design_efficiency()`
reports together with the upper bound of Patterson and Williams:

```{r}
al <- make_design("alpha", trt = 30, k = 5, r = 3, seed = 2026)
design_efficiency(al)[c("E", "upper_bound")]
```

Balanced incomplete blocks, Youden squares, cyclic designs and square
lattices are also available:

```{r}
design_efficiency(make_design("bib", trt = 7, k = 3, seed = 1))$E
plot(make_design("youden", trt = 7, k = 3, seed = 1))
```

## The field book

The field book has one row per plot, with the plot number, the field position,
the block and the treatment. Add the columns of the responses to be measured,
write it to CSV, and after the harvest it goes straight into `design_anova()`:

```{r}
book <- field_book(lay, c("Yield", "Height"))
head(book)
```

```r
field_book(lay, c("Yield", "Height"), file = "field-book.csv")
```
